A common path is: an associate or bachelor's degree in mechatronics or automation → commissioning assistant at an integrator or factory → electrician or industrial robot operation and maintenance certification → independent on-site engineer.

This work suits people who enjoy hands-on tasks, understand circuits, can read diagrams, and know how to tune parameters. If making equipment run steadily gives you a sense of achievement, this can be a stable career.

Robotics Technicians install, teach, calibrate, maintain, and troubleshoot industrial robots. They work with PLCs and machine vision to keep automated production lines running reliably and serve as core technical operations and maintenance personnel in smart manufacturing.

paragraphs: In the morning, first patrol the line and review alarm logs, resolving minor overnight shutdowns. Later, work with process engineers to teach pickup positions for a new product into the robotic arm and run dry cycles to eliminate interference. Around midday, use calibration tools to restore accuracy and integrate vision-based positioning. In the afternoon, secure a production window to replace wear parts and write maintenance records. Before leaving, prepare parameters for the new product variant scheduled for the next day.

In short: make industrial robots move correctly and reliably. Specific duties include installation, trajectory teaching, accuracy calibration, PLC and vision integration, troubleshooting, maintenance, writing SOPs, and training production-line workers. Combining analysis with hands-on work, robotics technicians are the front-line force of automation.

Simulation and vision-based calibration can instantly tune a robotic arm to a score of 90, but technicians still rely on their eyes and hands to decide how to grip a custom workpiece, shorten cycle time, and respond to unexpected problems on site.

Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) show that about 15,000 robotics technicians were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to rise to 15,100 by 2034, a net increase of about 100 jobs, with approximately 1,300 openings each year. The median annual wage was about $70,800 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace robotics technicians, but it will accelerate commissioning and diagnostics. Vision-based calibration, simulated offline programming, and remote diagnostics speed up repetitive work, shifting technicians from manual teaching toward process adaptation, custom integration, on-site emergency response, and predictive maintenance. People who only perform basic teaching and troubleshooting will be displaced, while those who can integrate systems and diagnose problems will become more valuable.

paragraphs: A score of 7/10 places this occupation in a moderately high AI-exposure category for commissioning work. Systems accelerate calibration, while integration and emergency response remain human responsibilities.

Moderately high exposure does not mean high risk. Basic teaching and troubleshooting tasks are being replaced, not roles centered on integration and diagnostics. Technicians with process insight who can rescue production on site become even scarcer as efficiency improves. Those who only follow manuals and press buttons face the greatest risk.

Build a foundation in mechatronics or automation and gain extensive hands-on experience with PLCs and teach pendants while in school. Basic teaching is contracting in the AI era, so develop integration and diagnostic skills early.
Advance from pressing buttons to integrating systems and troubleshooting faults. Learn machine vision, simulation, and predictive maintenance, and seek opportunities to lead on-site work.
Highlight commissioning and troubleshooting cases and clearly state which production lines you have supported. Factories value stability and speed.
Do not select candidates solely for installation skills; assess whether they can rescue production on site. Technicians capable of integration and diagnostics deserve substantial allowances.

This work suits people who combine hands-on ability, analytical thinking, and patience. Equipment must be functional and reliable, and circuits must be clearly diagnosed and effectively adjusted.

This field particularly develops the ability to use both hands and mind. You need to understand electrical systems, electronics, and PLCs while being willing to reach inside equipment to find faults. It suits people who enjoy disassembling things, analyzing how they work, and patiently tuning parameters.
A preference for hands-on work, investigation, and practicality (Realistic R + Investigative I + Conventional C).
If you enjoy analyzing how things work and use reliable equipment operation as your standard, robotics technician is one of manufacturing's most future-oriented technical entry points.

Technicians install, teach, and maintain robots so they can work reliably, focusing on on-site implementation. Electronics engineers design circuits and control-system solutions, focusing on research and development. One uses hands-on skills to keep operations running, while the other uses engineering analysis to define systems; both are indispensable.

subject.name: Robotics Technicians
subject.summary: Robotics technicians are the people who make robotic arms move as intended. They install, commission, and maintain industrial robots on production lines, turning a collection of automation components into a line that works reliably.
